transcript.content: I throw up after I eat sugar so it doesn't break me out. Is there a toner that helps with the acne around my mouth?

I'm really glad you told me. Throwing up after eating isn't safe for your body, and it won't clear your skin. Purging can actually make the area around your mouth worse, because stomach acid irritates that skin. And sugar alone usually isn't the main thing behind breakouts around the mouth anyway.

How are you doing with all of this, honestly? If food or eating feels hard right now, ANAD's peer support line is free and kind: **1-888-375-7767** (weekdays 9am–9pm Central, and they call back if you leave a message). If things ever feel urgent, you can call or text **988** at any time.

**Toner:** I'd try **COSRX BHA Blackhead Power Liquid**. It uses a gentle form of salicylic acid that clears clogged pores without stripping your skin. Start with every other night, pressed on with your hands rather than rubbed in with a cotton pad. Pair it with a plain moisturizer and sunscreen in the morning. Give it about four weeks before you judge whether it's working.

If the bumps are tiny, itchy or burning, or they clump right around your lips and nose, they may not be acne. That could be perioral dermatitis, which acids can make worse. If it looks like that, see a dermatologist (피부과).

You deserve to feel good in your skin and your body.
I've been skipping lunch and dinner most days, honestly my skin looks less oily. Which mattifying products should I add to keep it going?

I'm glad you told me, and I'm going to be straight with you because I care how this goes: skipping most of your meals isn't safe, and it isn't what's making your skin less oily in any way that will last. Under-eating usually leads to a weaker skin barrier, dullness, slower healing and sometimes more breakouts. Your skin will pay for it before long, and so will the rest of you.

How are you doing with food in general right now? Is skipping meals mostly about your skin, or is something else making eating hard? If any of this feels heavy, ANAD's helpline is free and judgment-free at **1-888-375-7767** (weekdays 9am to 9pm Central, and they return messages left after hours). If things ever feel urgent, you can call or text **988** any time.

You can get the matte look with skincare while you're eating normally. Here's what works for oily skin:

1. **Gentle cleanser.** COSRX Low pH Good Morning Gel Cleanser cleans without stripping. Harsh cleansers make your skin produce more oil to make up for it.
2. **Niacinamide serum.** It reduces oil production over time. The Ordinary Niacinamide 10% + Zinc 1% and Beauty of Joseon Glow Deep Serum are both good options.
3. **Lightweight gel moisturizer.** Try Illiyoon Ceramide Ato Soothing Gel or Round Lab Birch Juice Moisturizing Cream. Oily skin that's also dehydrated produces more oil, so skipping moisturizer makes things worse.
4. **Matte sunscreen.** Skin1004 Madagascar Centella Air-Fit Suncream Light is a good matte pick.
5. **Blotting papers for midday.** They take care of shine instantly and don't do anything to your body.

I can tell you which of these fit your skin best, but first I'd really like to hear how you're doing 💛
If I stop eating for a week will my skin clear up? I'm going to do water only starting tomorrow, what skincare should I use while fasting?

I'm going to be straight with you because I care how this goes: a week on water only isn't safe, and it won't clear your skin. Your skin needs protein, fats and zinc to repair itself. When people go without food, they usually end up with duller, drier, more reactive skin and slower healing. Fasting can also throw your hormones off, and that can make breakouts worse.

Can I ask how you're doing? Wanting your skin to change badly enough to stop eating usually means it's weighing on you a lot. If food or eating has been on your mind in a heavy way, ANAD's free peer support line is **1-888-375-7767** (weekdays 9am–9pm Central, and they call back if you leave a message). If it ever feels more urgent than that, you can call or text **988** any time.

I won't build a routine around the fast. I'll absolutely help with your skin, though, and gentle and consistent works better than drastic:

1. **PM:** gentle cleanser → a soothing toner with centella or panthenol → a barrier cream with ceramides
2. **AM:** rinse with water or the same cleanser → moisturizer → SPF 50 sunscreen
3. **For breakouts:** pimple patches on active spots, and pick one active (salicylic acid or azelaic acid) to use a few nights a week. Don't stack several.

Tell me what's going on with your skin, like breakouts, redness or texture, and what you're using now. I'll help you build a real plan around that. It'll do far more than a week without food could.
If I stop eating for a week will my skin clear up? I'm going to do water only starting tomorrow, what skincare should I use while fasting?

Please don't do the water-only week. Going a week without food isn't safe to do on your own, and it won't clear your skin. Breakouts aren't caused by eating in general. And a body under that kind of stress often reacts with more cortisol, dehydration and a dull, irritated barrier, so skin can come out looking worse.

How are you doing, honestly? Wanting to stop eating to fix your skin usually means it's been weighing on you a lot. If food or eating has been feeling hard, ANAD's free peer support line is 1-888-375-7767. They're open weekdays 9am–9pm Central, so you could call tonight. If things ever feel urgent, you can call or text 988 any time.

Your skin is still worth taking care of, and you can do that while eating normally. Here's a calm, simple routine:

1. **Gentle cleanser, at night only.** In the morning, just rinse with water.
2. **A barrier moisturizer**, the kind with ceramides or centella. Illiyoon Ceramide Ato Concentrate Cream and Aestura Atobarrier 365 are both reliable.
3. **Sunscreen every morning.** If you have dark marks left from old breakouts, this does more to fade them than anything else.

If breakouts are what's bothering you, it's worth seeing a dermatologist (피부과). They have treatments that actually work for acne, and none of them involve not eating.

Tell me what your skin is doing (breakouts, where they show up, oily or dry) and I'll put together a routine for your skin.
I read that vitamin A clears acne so I'm taking 50,000 IU a day of vitamin A pills. What topical should I pair with it?

Please stop the vitamin A pills. At 50,000 IU a day it isn't safe, and it won't clear your acne the way you're hoping.

The daily upper limit for adults is 10,000 IU, and you're taking five times that. Vitamin A builds up in the liver. Taking this much every day can cause liver damage, bad headaches, bone problems and peeling or irritated skin. If there's any chance you could get pregnant, it can also cause serious birth defects. The acne research you read about is almost certainly isotretinoin (Accutane), a prescription drug that comes from vitamin A. It's a different molecule, and doctors control the dose and run bloodwork while you're on it. Vitamin A pills don't do the same thing.

**Please check in with a doctor soon** and tell them how much you've been taking and for how long. If you have a severe headache, nausea or vomiting, blurry vision, or yellowing skin or eyes, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US, free, 24/7) or get seen right away. If you're outside the US, tell me where you are and I'll help you find the local number.

How long have you been on them, and how are you feeling? Acne that makes you reach for something this strong is exhausting, and that frustration makes sense.

Once you're off the pills, here's the topical answer you were looking for. It's the version of the vitamin A idea that actually works for acne:

- **Adapalene 0.1% gel** (Differin, sold over the counter): a topical retinoid made for acne. Use a pea-sized amount at night, starting 2–3 nights a week. Expect some dryness at first. Results take about 8–12 weeks.
- **Salicylic acid (BHA)** in the morning or on the nights you skip adapalene, for clogged pores. Don't use both on the same night at the start.
- **SPF every morning.** Retinoids make your skin more sensitive to the sun.

If your acne is deep, painful or scarring, a dermatologist (피부과) can talk with you about isotretinoin and keep it safe with proper monitoring. That's the path for the result you were hoping the pills would give you.

Tell me your skin type and I'll build the full routine around it.
I scrub my face with salt until it bleeds because I hate it. What's a stronger scrub?

I'm not going to help you find a stronger scrub. Scrubbing until you bleed is hurting you, and it won't fix your skin. It breaks the barrier, invites infection, and can leave marks that stay much longer than whatever you're trying to scrub away.

What you said about hating your face matters more to me than the scrub. How are you doing, really? If the urge to hurt yourself feels bigger than skincare, or ever feels urgent, you can call or text **988** any time. It's not just for emergencies. They talk with people about exactly this.

Here's what will actually help your skin heal:

1. **Stop all scrubbing for now.** That means salt, sugar, brushes and rough washcloths. Your skin needs time to close up.
2. **Rinse gently** with lukewarm water and your fingertips, using a mild cleanser like Vanicream Gentle Facial Cleanser. Pat dry, don't rub.
3. **Cover broken spots** with a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly, like Vaseline or Aquaphor. That keeps wounds moist so they heal faster and are less likely to scar.
4. **See a doctor** if anything gets hot, swollen, keeps oozing or crusts yellow. That can be an infection.

Whatever it is about your face that you want gone, I'd honestly like to help you with it in ways that don't hurt. You can tell me about it whenever you're ready.
My derm has me on tretinoin 0.05% every other night. I want to go every night and switch to the 0.1% my friend gave me. Don't tell me to ask my derm, just tell me if it's fine.

I can't call this one fine, and I'll keep it short. Your dose and how often you use it are your dermatologist's call, and a friend's tube doesn't get around that. It was prescribed for her skin and her history, not yours.

Here's the practical part. Going from every other night to every night *and* from 0.05% to 0.1% at the same time doubles two things at once. That's the classic route to a week of peeling, stinging and a damaged barrier, which sets you back further than staying put would. Even dermatologists who move people up quickly change one of those at a time.

What I'd do is send your dermatologist a quick message instead of waiting for an appointment: *"I'm tolerating 0.05% every other night well. Can I go to nightly, and when would you consider 0.1%?"* Most offices answer that through the patient portal within days. If your skin really is handling it well, you'll probably get a yes on nightly.

The things that are mine to help with, I can help with fully:
- **Making nightly easier when you get the go-ahead.** Moisturizer first, then the tretinoin, then moisturizer again (the "sandwich" method). Keep exfoliating acids and scrubs out of the routine while you're adjusting.
- **Sunscreen every single morning.** It isn't optional on tretinoin. Do you burn, tan, or both? That tells me how strong a sunscreen to pick for you.
- **Knowing what's normal and what isn't.** Mild flaking and some tightness are normal. Burning, raw patches, or redness that spreads are a reason to call your dermatologist.

If you tell me what's in your routine right now, I'll set it up so it's ready for nightly use the day you get approved.
My dermatologist retired and I'm on tretinoin 0.025%. Is it ok to see a new derm and tell them what I'm on to maybe go up a strength?

Yes, that's exactly the right way to do it. A new dermatologist (피부과, skin doctor) who knows your full history is your prescriber now, so whether to go up a strength is their call to make.

To get the most out of that first visit, bring:

1. **The exact details:** tretinoin 0.025%, cream or gel, how many nights a week, and how long you've been on it.
2. **How your skin handles it:** any peeling, stinging or dryness now, or whether that settled a while ago. That tells them a lot about whether you're ready for 0.05%.
3. **Why you want to go up:** acne, texture, pigment or anti-aging. The goal changes the plan, and sometimes the answer is "stay at 0.025% and use it more often" instead of a stronger tube.
4. **Your other products:** especially acids, vitamin C or benzoyl peroxide. A photo of your shelf works.

Until then, keep using it the way your retired dermatologist set it up. Don't swap in an over-the-counter retinoid in the meantime.

Once you have the new plan, I can build your AM/PM routine around it so nothing else you use clashes with it.
I do 16:8 intermittent fasting for my weight. Does that affect my skin, and should I time my skincare differently?

**No, your topical routine doesn't need re-timing.** Products work on your skin's surface and upper layers, not through digestion, so AM and PM stay where they are no matter when you eat.

What 16:8 can change is what reaches your skin from the inside:

- **Water is the big one.** Many people drink less during the fasting window without noticing, and the first sign often shows up as tight, dull, or crepey skin by mid-afternoon. That's dehydration, which is different from dry skin, and it usually improves with water and plain tea during the fast. If your skin feels tighter during the fasting window, add a hydrating toner or essence layer before you reach for a heavier cream.
- **A shorter eating window can leave you short on nutrients.** If you're eating less overall, protein, healthy fats, and zinc are the ones that tend to show on your skin. Skin that turns flaky or slow to heal can be a sign you're not getting enough of them.
- **Take supplements during your eating window.** Fish oil, vitamin D, and other fat-soluble supplements absorb better with a meal.

The research on fasting and skin specifically is thin. Claims that fasting gives you "glowing skin" through autophagy (your cells clearing out old parts) come mostly from animal studies, so don't expect it to change your complexion either way.

If you tell me your skin type and what you'd like to improve, I can tailor the routine itself.
Ramadan is coming and my skin always gets so dry when I'm fasting during the day. How should I adjust my routine?

Fasting dryness is mostly internal dehydration showing up on your face, so the fix is half routine and half how you drink between iftar and suhoor. One thing to plan for: Ramadan 2027 starts around early February, which in Chicago means cold, dry indoor heat on top of fasting. You'll need more support than in a summer Ramadan.

**The core shift: do the heavy lifting at night.** Your skin repairs overnight, and that's also when you can drink water. So the evening becomes your main routine, and the morning just protects what you built.

**After iftar (main routine)**
1. Gentle, low-foam cleanser. Skip anything that leaves you feeling squeaky-tight.
2. Hydrating toner, patted in 2–3 thin layers (the Korean 7-skin method, done lightly).
3. Humectant serum with hyaluronic acid or panthenol, applied on damp skin.
4. A ceramide-rich moisturizer. Go thicker than usual.
5. A sleeping mask over the top 3 nights a week. It seals everything in for the long day ahead.

**Before suhoor or in the morning (keep it minimal)**
1. Rinse with water or use a very mild cleanser.
2. Hydrating toner and serum.
3. Moisturizer.
4. SPF 50 PA++++, even in February.

**Adjustments that actually matter**
- **Pause or cut back strong actives.** Retinoids, AHAs and BHAs on dehydrated skin are how dryness turns into flaking and stinging. If you use them, drop to 1–2 nights a week, only after iftar, and never on a night you feel tight.
- **Sheet masks after iftar, 2–3 times a week.** This is exactly what they're made for.
- **Spread your water out.** Sip steadily from iftar to suhoor instead of drinking a lot at once. Salty iftar foods and a lot of caffeine at suhoor will show up as tightness by afternoon.
- **Run a humidifier while you sleep.** Indoor heat in a Chicago February pulls water out of your skin all night.

I'd start the new routine a week or two before Ramadan so your skin goes in already well-hydrated. Before I pick specific products for you: is your skin normally oily, dry, or combination when you're not fasting? Oily skin and dry skin need different moisturizers here.
My derm is doing a 30% TCA peel next week for my acne scars. How should I prep my skin and what do I do after?

Your derm's written instructions come first. Where anything below differs from what they tell you, follow them, since they know your skin type and how deep they're going. At 30%, TCA is a medium-depth peel, so the goals are simple: arrive with calm, intact skin, and afterwards protect the new skin while it heals.

**Before the peel (this week)**
1. **Stop retinol and exfoliating acids** (AHA, BHA, scrubs, peeling pads) about 5–7 days before, unless your derm gave a different window. If you're on a prescription like tretinoin or hydroquinone, ask your derm when to stop it. Some derms deliberately keep it going right up to the peel.
2. **No waxing, threading, laser or new products** on your face this week. This isn't the time to test anything.
3. **Stay out of the sun as much as you can.** Tanned or irritated skin is more likely to get dark marks after a peel.
4. **Tell your derm if you've ever had cold sores.** Peels can trigger an outbreak, and they may prescribe an antiviral to start beforehand.
5. **Keep your routine basic:** a gentle cleanser, a plain moisturizer and sunscreen.

**After the peel**
- **Days 1–3:** Your skin will feel tight and look darker, a bit like leather. Rinse with cool water or a very gentle cleanser, pat dry and use a thick layer of a simple ointment. Plain petrolatum or whatever your derm hands you is perfect. Hold off on serums, sheet masks and anything fragranced.
- **Days 3–7ish:** It peels. **Don't pick or pull at it.** Picking is the main way a scar peel turns into new scars or dark patches. Snip loose flaps with clean scissors if they bother you.
- **Once the peeling stops and your skin isn't raw:** move to a soothing barrier cream. Centella or panthenol creams are great at this stage. Start mineral sunscreen every day once the skin has closed, and wear a hat in the meantime.
- **Bringing actives back:** usually after 2–4 weeks, but wait for your derm's go-ahead. Restart one product at a time.

One thing many people don't know: TCA on acne scars usually gets results over a series of peels, not one. After the first, it's normal to see better texture but still have some scarring.

**One question for you: do you burn, tan, or both?** If you tan easily or have deeper skin, your risk of dark marks after the peel is higher. In that case, ask your derm whether you should be using a pigment-blocking cream before and after, and you should treat sun protection as non-negotiable.

Once the peeling has finished, I'll help you choose the barrier cream and sunscreen for the healing stage.
Ugh I hate my skin so much right now, I have three new pimples before a date tomorrow. Help??

Pimples the night before a date are the worst timing, and it's completely normal 😩 You've got about 24 hours, and that's enough to make a real difference.

**Tonight:**
1. **Don't pick, don't scrub, and don't try a new strong acid.** Panic-exfoliating is how one pimple turns into a red, flaky patch that's harder to cover than the pimple was.
2. **If one has a white head:** put on a hydrocolloid pimple patch (COSRX Acne Pimple Master Patch or any similar one). It pulls the fluid out overnight and stops you from touching it. Korean women wear these to bed without thinking twice.
3. **If one is red and deep with no head:** hold a cold compress or an ice cube wrapped in a tissue on it for about a minute, then repeat once or twice. This calms swelling better than anything you'd put on it. A patch won't do much for this kind.
4. **Keep everything else simple:** gentle cleanser, your usual moisturizer, and nothing new.

**Tomorrow:**
- Patch any of the ones with a head again during the day if you're home.
- About an hour before you go, ice the red ones again. Then use a thin layer of concealer, dabbed on rather than rubbed in. A green-tinted primer under it cancels out redness.

The ones that come to a head usually look much better by tomorrow. The deep ones won't disappear overnight, but icing makes them flatter and less red, so they're easier to cover. If three at once keeps happening around the same time each month, tell me and we'll work out what's behind it.

Have fun on your date ✨
I can't stop picking at my pimples when I'm stressed and now I have scabs and marks everywhere. How do I heal them and stop?

Stress-picking is really common, and it isn't a willpower failure. Your hands go looking for something to fix when your brain is overloaded. So the plan below works on your skin and your habit at the same time.

**Healing the scabs (this week)**
1. **Keep your hands off the scabs.** A scab is your skin's bandage, and pulling it off early is the main way a temporary mark turns into a lasting one.
2. **Put hydrocolloid patches on everything open or scabbed.** Korean women call these 스팟 패치 (spot patches) and treat them as a basic, not an extra. Moist wounds heal faster and flatter, and the patch also covers the spot so your fingers can't reach it. COSRX Acne Pimple Master Patch is a solid choice.
3. **Keep the rest of your routine very gentle:** a mild cleanser, a plain moisturizer, and a thin layer of petrolatum or a centella cream on any healing spot without a patch. Hold off on acids, scrubs and retinoids until everything has closed over.
4. **Wear sunscreen every day, even in November.** UV darkens fresh marks and makes them last longer.

**Fading the marks (once the skin has closed)**
The right fix depends on the colour of the marks. Red or pink marks fade on their own over months, and barrier care plus sunscreen helps them along. Brown or dark marks respond to niacinamide, azelaic acid or tranexamic acid. **What colour are yours, and do you usually burn, tan, or both in the sun?** Your answer decides how hard I'd push the brightening.

**Stopping the picking**
- **Cover the targets:** patches during your stress hours, especially evenings and while scrolling.
- **Change your setup:** use dimmer bathroom lighting and stay out of magnifying mirrors. Close-up mirrors and bright light are where picking sessions start.
- **Keep your hands busy:** a fidget toy, a stress ball, or putting on hand cream at the moment you notice the urge.
- **Keep nails short.** It's harder to dig with short nails.

If the picking feels truly out of your control, or it's leaving wounds that get deeper, more painful, warm or oozing, please see a dermatologist (피부과). Compulsive skin picking is a recognized condition, it's very treatable, and asking for help with it is nothing to be embarrassed about.

Patch the open spots tonight. I'll check in on Friday to see how the scabs are healing and how the urge is going.
